docs.title: SAR Drone Build Log
docs.text:
I'm Joseph Kim, a UIUC sophomore and a beginner in AI. This site documents an aerial casualty-location proof of concept I'm building for the Cozad New Venture Competition.

The project has two chapters:

  • Chapter 1: Search Path plans a "lawnmower" flight path so the drone photographs the whole search area with no gaps.
  • Chapter 2: Person Detection scans those photos and flags likely people for a human to review.

Prototype, not a product

These tools are early experiments. Read the Limits page before drawing conclusions.

Updates and lessons learned go in the Blog. New terms are defined in the Glossary.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Search path
docs.text:
Lawnmower path — A flight path of straight lines back and forth across an area, like mowing a lawn. Also called a boustrophedon or parallel-track search.

Lane — One straight line of the lawnmower path.

Waypoint — A GPS point the drone flies to. A path is a list of waypoints.

Field of view (FOV) — The angle the camera can see, in degrees. Wider FOV = bigger photo on the ground.

Footprint — The patch of ground one photo covers. Grows with flight height and FOV.

Sidelap — How much neighboring lanes' photos overlap side to side, as a percent. Prevents gaps.

Lane spacing — The distance between lanes. Footprint width × (1 − sidelap).

docs.title: Chapter 2: Person detection
docs.text:
Bounding box — A rectangle the model draws around something it thinks it found.

Confidence score — A number from 0 to 1 showing how sure the model is about one box. Not a probability of being right.

Threshold — The minimum confidence score I keep. Lower = more boxes, more false alarms. Higher = fewer boxes, more misses.

False positive — The model flags a person where there isn't one (e.g., a bush or a bag).

Missed detection (false negative) — A real person the model did not flag.

Ground truth — The correct answer, marked by a human, used to check the model.

Inference — Running a trained model on new images to get predictions.

YOLO — "You Only Look Once," a family of fast object-detection models.

Ultralytics — The Python library I use to run YOLO models.

VisDrone — A public dataset of drone images with labeled people and vehicles. Used to train the model I use.

Fine-tuning — Training an existing model a bit more on a specific dataset.

SAHI — "Slicing Aided Hyper Inference." Cuts a large image into smaller overlapping tiles, runs the model on each, then merges the results. Helps find small objects.

Tile / slice — One small piece of the big image.

Overlap — How much neighboring tiles share, so a person on a tile edge isn't cut in half.

RGB — A normal color photo (red, green, blue). Not thermal or night imagery.

Last updated: 2026-10-28

Not for real search-and-rescue use

These are proof-of-concept tools. Do not use them to make real search decisions.

docs.title: Tool 2 — person detector
docs.text:
• Tiny test set: tested on 2 images, tuned on 1 of them. Results may not repeat on other images.
  • Daylight RGB only: not tested on night, thermal, fog, smoke, snow, or heavy tree cover.
  • No accuracy claim: I don't report accuracy yet. I report counts of false positives and missed detections instead.
  • Human in the loop: the tool flags likely people for a person to review. It does not confirm anyone.
  • Training data bias: the model learned from VisDrone (mostly urban scenes in China). Rural fields and forests may look different to it.
  • Altitude and resolution: results depend on drone height, camera, and image size. Not tested across these.

docs.title: Finding people in drone images: what worked and what didn't
docs.text:
A drone photo taken from high up can cover a whole field, but a person in it may be only a few pixels wide. I built a small tool to flag likely people for a human to review. Here's what worked, what didn't, and what I still don't know.

Status

Prototype. Tested on 2 daylight RGB images, tuned on 1. See Limits.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: In search and rescue (SAR), a drone can photograph a large area fast. The slow part is a person staring at hundreds of images looking for someone small. My goal: flag spots worth a second look, so the human reviews fewer areas. The human still decides.

docs.title: What I used
docs.text:
• Ultralytics — a Python library that runs YOLO, a fast object detector.
  • VisDrone — a public dataset of drone images with labeled people. The model I used was trained on it, so it has seen people from above.
  • SAHI — cuts a big image into smaller overlapping tiles, runs the detector on each, then merges the boxes.

New terms are in the Glossary.

docs.title: Attempt 2: slice the image with SAHI
docs.text:
The key block (simplified from my notebook):

from sahi import AutoDetectionModel
from sahi.predict import get_sliced_prediction

model = AutoDetectionModel.from_pretrained(
    model_type="ultralytics",
    model_path="visdrone_model.pt",   # [replace with my model]
    confidence_threshold=0.3,         # [my value]
)

result = get_sliced_prediction(
    "drone_image.jpg",
    model,
    slice_height=640, slice_width=640,                  # tile size
    overlap_height_ratio=0.2, overlap_width_ratio=0.2,  # 20% overlap
)

What it does:

  • The model block loads the detector and sets the threshold: boxes below this confidence are dropped.
  • The slice block cuts the image into 640×640 tiles. Each tile is closer to the size the model expects, so small people stay big enough to see.
  • The overlap (20%) means a person on a tile edge appears in two tiles and isn't cut in half. SAHI then merges duplicate boxes.

docs.text:

  • Night, thermal, smoke, or forest cover — untested.
  • Whether my threshold is a good trade-off between misses and false alarms. In SAR, a miss is usually worse than a false alarm, but too many false alarms waste reviewer time.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Planning the drone's search path
docs.text:
Update (Nov 2026)

I later made search_v2.py reusable so other scripts can import its functions. The input() lines moved under if __name__ == "__main__":, and save_gpx now takes start_lat and start_lon as parameters. The logic and the output are unchanged. Explained in Chapter 3.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
After interviewing SAR team leads at Illinois several key issues were identified: - Lack of volunteers - Time issue narrowing down search areas

The current breakdown of chain of command: Command centers give designated search areas to local SAR teams -> SAR teams search areas -> come back to command center to find a new search area. Inevitably SAR teams (K9 dogs & SAR volunteers) are irreplaceable. Drones could pre-scan an area and flag likely spots, helping teams decide where to search first.

This section is dedicated in creating flight patterns for the drone to scan an area beforehand.

flowchart TD
    A[You type 6 inputs] --> B[make_lawnmower]

docs.title: Step 1: Inputs
docs.text:
import math

Allows us to use built in math functions such as math.cos, math.ceil, math.pi and more

START_LAT = float(input("Start latitude: "))
START_LON = float(input("Start longitude: "))
WIDTH_M = float(input("Search area width, east-west, in meters: "))
HEIGHT_M = float(input("Search area height, north-south, in meters: "))
LANE_SPACING_M = float(input("Lane spacing in meters: "))
SPEED_MPS = float(input("Drone speed (m/s): "))
OUTPUT_FILE = "search_route.gpx"
  • These are inputs, not results. When the program starts, it would ask you to type 6 values: start point (latitude and longitude), search width, height, lane spacing, and speed. It'll be helpful if we can command the drones to search on its own in the future if we have an input function like so.

The very last code lets us set the name of the output file.

METERS_PER_DEG_LAT = 111_320
  • A constant: convert between GPS degrees and meters. 111,320 m per degree of latitude. Therefore, we use this conversion. _ is simply used for readability.

docs.title: Step 2: Building the lanes
docs.text:
def make_lawnmower(width, height, spacing):
    lanes = math.ceil(width / spacing) + 1
    points = []
    for i in range(lanes):
        east = min(i * spacing, width)
        if i % 2 == 0:
            points.append((east, 0))
            points.append((east, height))
        else:
            points.append((east, height))
            points.append((east, 0))
    return points
  • The image one of the SAR team leads showed me for the search areas appeared to be a rectangle. Therefore, we also used rectangles to replicate search areas.
  • Lanes account for the number of lanes = field width / lane spacing, rounded up +1.
  • Spacing realistically would be represented how wide a strip of ground the camera sees minus the overlap. +1 accounts for the beginning of the count. Just like how a 30m fence with post every 10m has 4 posts and 3 gaps. The posts would represent the lanes.
  • points = []: the coordinates go in it. It is empty because the function hasn't calculated any waypoints yet, and the loop fills it.
  • for i in range(lanes): One per lane; i counts 0, 1, 2...
  • east = min(i * spacing, width): i * spacing represents how far the lane is from the starting edge. By the time it reaches outside the search area, the min(..., width) picks the smaller number so the last lane gets pulled back to the fields edge.
  • if i % 2 == 0: :Change drones direction depending on whether it is on a even/odd lane so that the drone doesn't reposition itself facing the same direction every time it clears a lane, it'll be a waste of time having the drone set up its position after every lane.
  • Without a flip, the drone will fly all the way across the field to start again = waste of battery and time.
  • return points : hands back full list of planned way points.
def to_lat_lon(east_m, north_m, start_lat, start_lon):
    lat = start_lat + north_m / METERS_PER_DEG_LAT
    meters_per_deg_lon = METERS_PER_DEG_LAT * math.cos(math.radians(start_lat))
    lon = start_lon + east_m / meters_per_deg_lon
    return lat, lon
  • we need this function because our waypoints are in meters, but GPS or a map needs the waypoints converted to lat, lon values
  • lat = ... 111,320 / 111,320 to get 1 degree north. Then the code adds that to start_lat to get the new latitude.
  • Near the poles, 1 degree of longitude covers fewer meters, so the meters_per_deg_lon gets smaller. So even if the same distance of 100m may be covered, it would result in more degrees of longitude. Urbana is around 40 degrees north, so cos(40) ~ 0.77. If we multiply that by 111,320 we get 85,000m in Urbana.
  • converts latitude values to radians so it can be used to be calculated using the cos function
  • hands back the latitude and longitude of one waypoint. Used by save_gpx.

def path_length(points):
    total = 0
    for (x1, y1), (x2, y2) in zip(points, points[1:]):
        total += math.hypot(x2 - x1, y2 - y1)
    return total
- This determines the length of the path. We start with 0 as our total. - zip(points, points[1:]) : pairs each waypoint with the next one, so each pair is one leg of the flight. - The math.hypot function turns two changes (east and north values) into one straight line distance. - The += function acts as an odometer, additional gain. This allows the main block to divide total distance by drone speed. - Example: (0,0) --> (0,100) = 100m, (0,100) --> (30,100) = 30m, so the total distance goes from 0 --> 100 --> 130.

def save_gpx(points, filename):
    lines = ['<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>',
             '<gpx version="1.1" creator="search_pattern.py" '
             'xmlns="http://www.topografix.com/GPX/1/1">',
             ' <rte>',
             ' <name>Lawnmower search</name>']
    for east, north in points:
        lat, lon = to_lat_lon(east, north, START_LAT, START_LON)
        lines.append(f' <rtept lat="{lat:.6f}" lon="{lon:.6f}"/>')
    lines += [' </rte>', '</gpx>']
    with open(filename, "w") as f:
        f.write("\n".join(lines))
  • <rte> indicates where route section starts in the file and </rte> marks where it ends. <name> gives it name.
  • <?xml...> and <gpx...> acts as headers that tells apps that it is a start of GPX file.
  • for east, north in points: takes one meter waypoint at a time
  • to_lat_lon(...) convert it to GPS latitude and longitude
  • lines.append(...) adds one <rtept> route point line with those numbers
  • lines += [...] adds the closing tags </rte> and </gpx> to end the route and the file.
  • open(filename, "w") creates the file. "w" means write, and it replaces any old file with the same name.
  • "\n".join(lines) puts each line on its own row.
  • We save gpx points so it can be reopened using Google Earth and show the route on a real map or load it.
  • 1 decimal place is 11km so rounding to 6 decimal places helps us narrow down the precision to 10cm
if __name__ == "__main__":
    route = make_lawnmower(WIDTH_M, HEIGHT_M, LANE_SPACING_M)
    distance = path_length(route)
    minutes = distance / SPEED_MPS / 60
    area_hectares = WIDTH_M * HEIGHT_M / 10_000

    save_gpx(route, OUTPUT_FILE)
    print(f"Area: {area_hectares:.1f} hectares")
    print(f"Waypoints: {len(route)}")
    print(f"Path length: {distance:.0f} m")
    print(f"Estimated flight time: {minutes:.1f} minutes")
    print(f"Saved route to {OUTPUT_FILE}")
  • if __name__ == "__main__": means running the part only when the file is started directly, acts as the program start button, calls the functions defined above.
  • minutes : distance/speed gives seconds of flight time. Dividing by 60 turns seconds into minutes.
  • area_hectares divide by 10,000 since one hectare is 10,000m^2, dividing by 10000 converts units back to hectares.
  • saves the gpx values so it can be reopened in different maps if necessary
  • prints the number of waypoints while len() is used to count them
  • prints planned distance, since the drone hasn't flown yet.
  • prints flight time How I checked it:
  • Ran it with a 200 × 100 m area and 30 m spacing: 16 waypoints, 1,000 m path.
  • Worked the distance math by hand (0 → 100 → 130 m).

What I don't understand yet - Exact GPX format rules

docs.title: Chapter 2: Finding people in drone photos
The problem
docs.text: Drones can photograph a search area in minutes, but finding a tiny person in hundreds of photos is slow, so this tool flags the photos most likely to show someone, so the SAR team knows where to look first.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text: Step Where Link Train VisDrone model Colab Train HERIDAL model Colab Run detection My laptop

docs.title: Step 1: Plain YOLO (detect.py)
docs.text:
from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolov8n.pt")
results = model("images/test2.jpg", classes=[0], conf=0.15, imgsz=1280, iou=0.5)
print("People found:", len(results[0].boxes))
results[0].save("outputs/out.jpg")
- print("People found:", len(results[0].boxes)) Counts the number of boxes detected. The boxes each have a confidence score from 0 to 1 and each box marks a suspected person. YOLO returns a list of results, so [0] picks the first and only result. Since python counts from 0, the first item is 0. Some boxes may be on bushes or shadows, and some people may be missed. - results = model("images/test2.jpg", classes=[0], conf=0.15, imgsz=1280, iou=0.5) if the model knows 80 kind of objects, class 0 represents person in COCO (dataset this model learned from) it is trying to find. Trade off: 0.15 is low, bringing more false alarms. SAR uses this as a missing person is worse than a false alarm. Boxes below 0.15 are dropped and don't get to have a box created around it. The model shrinks every photo to this size before looking at it. Bigger size images keeps more pixels, allowing a tiny hiker stay big enough for recognition. The program runs slower, however. If two boxes over lap more than 50%, the model keeps the one with the higher confidence and removes the other. from ultralytics import YOLO - It loads the YOLO tool from Ultralytics library. model = YOLO("yolov8n.pt") - n in yolov8n represents nano. The speed is fastest, but has the lowest accuracy. I started with the smallest model because I was running the tests on a laptop, not a GPU. There are bigger sizes for yolov8 that runs more accurate, but slower. results[0].save("outputs/out.jpg") - It saves one image, with the boxes and confidence scores drawn on it.

docs.title: Step 2: Slicing with SAHI (detect_sahi.py)
docs.text:
from sahi import AutoDetectionModel
from sahi.predict import get_sliced_prediction

model = AutoDetectionModel.from_pretrained(
    model_type="ultralytics",
    model_path="visdrone_yolov8s.pt",
    confidence_threshold=0.2,
    device="cpu",
)

result = get_sliced_prediction(
    "images/test4.jpg",
    model,
    slice_height=640,
    slice_width=640,
    overlap_height_ratio=0.4,
    overlap_width_ratio=0.4,
)

result.object_prediction_list = [
    p for p in result.object_prediction_list if p.category.id in (0,1)
]

scores = sorted((p.score.value for p in result.object_prediction_list), reverse=True)
print(scores[:10])

print("People found:", len(result.object_prediction_list))
result.export_visuals(export_dir="outputs/", file_name="sahi_s_test4_192_020")
